title: Green Hydrogen Supply Chains and Organizational Performance in MENA Oil and Gas Firms: A Natural Resource-Based View of Managerial and Technological Barriers
content: The worldwide push towards decarbonization has placed green hydrogen at the foundation of sustainable energy transitions, particularly in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, where oil and gas corporations are expanding into low-carbon directions. Grounded in the Natural Resource-Based View (NRBV) and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study addresses whether green hydrogen supply chain initiatives can translate into competitive organizational performance in emerging market contexts characterized by managerial and technological constraints. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, data were collected from 510 oil and gas professionals in the MENA region and analyzed through covariance-based structural equation modelling (CB-SEM). The findings indicate that green supply chain practices, specifically regulatory compliance and waste management, have a strong positive impact on organizational performance, while both managerial and technological barriers exert significant negative effects. Moderation analysis reveals an important asymmetry: technological barriers significantly condition the green practice-performance relationship, whereas managerial barriers, though directly harmful to performance, do not significantly moderate that pathway. This asymmetry is interpreted through a DCT lens: it is not green investment per se, but rather a firm's dynamic capacity to sense, seize, and reconfigure resources around those investments, enabled by technological infrastructure that determines whether NRBV-predicted performance advantages are realized. This study makes an original contribution by being among the first to empirically test the NRBV in the context of green hydrogen supply chains, and advances theory by demonstrating that the NRBV's performance logic is contingent on organizational enabling conditions, specifically technological readiness, as a scope condition rather than a mere empirical moderator.
